newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian regulatory row threatens depository plan.
newsitem.headline: Russian regulatory row threatens depository plan.

text.p: A row between Russia's central bank and a key securities industry watchdog is threatening plans for a central share depository, which supporters say will boost investment in stocks and strengthen investor protection.

The Federal Commission for the Securities Market earlier this month adopted temporary regulations on centralising depository activities and licensed several regional depositories as part of the network.
"We believe the creation of a central depository system will facilitate dealing with Russia's best blue chips," commission chairman Dmitry Vasilyev told a news conference on Tuesday.
The lack of developed infrastructure, including back office functions such as depository services and clearing, has been seen as a major obstacle to investment in Russian shares.
A working group from Vasilyev's commission has been given a month to determine how the depository would work.
Vasilyev said the adoption of a unified system would put Russia on a par with other countries and help protect property rights.
But he also cautioned that a unified system could only be created with central bank cooperation.
"The creation of a central depository will only be possible if the central bank stops its claims to the monopolisation of all decisions on the capital market."
Otherwise there would be two depositories -- one for shares and one for government securities.

Central Bank First Deputy Chairman Sergei Aleksashenko was quick to respond, saying in a statement on Tuesday the temporary regulations partially contradicted the criminal code and securities market law.
The regulations also gave the commission powers which were not envisaged in law, Aleksashenko said.
"The central bank officially declares that it has never claimed and does not claim a monopoly on regulation of the capital market," the statement said.
Bank and commission have clashed before. In September 1995, bank deputy chairman Andrei Kozlov called for Vasilyev to resign, saying comments he made had undermined the bank.
Kozlov said a report by Vasilyev accused the central bank of concealing information about the T-bill market.
The row appeared settled a few days later when the commission issued a statement of support for bank policies.
But the central bank has since made clear it would like to regulate banks' activities in the securities market.
The status of the commission also appeared to be in doubt earlier this year. In the wake of the presidential election, it was briefly downgraded, sparking fears it could lose its regulatory powers.
In less than five years, Russia has developed a national electronic over-the counter trading system and tackled many infrastructural problems which hit investors in the early days.
The Depositary Clearing Company (DCC), set up by leading brokerages in 1994, has provided settlement services but president Mikhail Lelyavsky said a unified system was required.
"There is a trading system which allows the regions to take part in trading sessions but it is impossible to settle up with them in a unified system," he said.
He said the stock market was starting to fulfill its primary role of financing the restructuring of privatised companies.
"The volume of this financing will to a great extent be determined by the available infrastructure."
--Nigel Stephenson, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
